blocks.text: Subject: Thank you for coming in, and what happens next
Dear Avery,
Thank you for making the time to come and see us. It was good to talk through the £100,000 sitting in your savings account, and your feeling that it should be working harder than it is.
Here is a short recap of what we covered.
Why you got in touch: you want to know whether retiring at 67 is realistic, and you want a plan for the £100,000 rather than a one-off answer.

What you told us you hold: a workplace pension of roughly £111,226, and cash savings of about £110,867 in total, of which you regard £10,867 as money you will not touch. These are the figures you gave us from memory, so we will verify them before anything else happens.
Your time horizon: around 22 years.
What you asked for: someone to keep an eye on the plan over time, not just a single recommendation.

How we work: we explained our service, the difference between advice and information, and that no recommendation was given in the meeting. A recommendation only follows a full fact find and a risk assessment. You have the Terms of Business and our fee schedule, which set out our initial and ongoing charges.
We also agreed the next steps.
You: let me know if the fact find raises any questions when you read it through, and confirm you are happy for us to contact your pension provider.
Me: send you the fact find and the attitude to risk questionnaire within the next two working days.
You: complete and return both when you have a spare half hour. Please aim for two weeks if you can.
Me: send you the authority form to approach your existing pension provider for full plan details, alongside the fact find.
Me: request those plan details once the authority is signed, then confirm a date to report back to you with a written recommendation.

The Groundwork Report is our entry service. It is an advised initial financial plan and sense check, covering your objectives and your existing arrangements. The fee is £2,000, and it is refunded or offset against initial advice if you take full regulated advice from us within 12 months. Our Terms of Business set out the full detail here: [TO CONFIRM: insert Terms of Business link]
I have also enclosed our Welcome Guide and our Financial Well-Being Checklist. The checklist is a simple way to spot anything we have not yet talked about.
Nothing is committed at this stage, and you are under no obligation to proceed. If anything in the paperwork is unclear, please just ask.
I look forward to hearing from you.

Why you got in touch

You had £100,000 sitting in a savings account earning very little. In your words, it "should be doing something". You did not know where to start, and you did not want to take a risk you could not live with.

Alongside that, you wanted a straight answer to a bigger question: are you on track to retire comfortably? You had built up a workplace pension over your working life but had never had anyone look at the whole picture with you.
You were clear that you were not looking for a one-off tip. You wanted someone to keep an eye on things over time.

A view on retiring at 67. You wanted to know whether that is realistic given what you have already built up and what you can add.

We do not advise on defined-benefit, or final salary, pension transfers.

We arrange mortgages for existing financial-planning clients only.

Our planning is built around your goals rather than around products, and it is designed to run across your working life and into retirement. Our service is staged, our fees are set out in writing, and there is no obligation to proceed at any point.

Our entry service is the Groundwork Report. It is an advised service. It produces an initial holistic financial plan and a sense check of what you already hold. The fee is £2,000. blocks.text: Your objectives

You told me you want to know whether you are on track to retire comfortably. That is the reason you came to me now, and it is the reason you want this £100,000 put to work rather than left in the bank.
Your objectives, as you described them:
Invest £100,000 for the long term, towards retirement at 67. That is 22 years from now, and it sets the investment term.
Reach a retirement income of £28,500 a year from age 67, which you described as about 60% of your current income.
Keep your £10,867 emergency fund in cash, separate from anything invested. You did not want to invest money you might need at short notice.
Use tax allowances you are not currently using, in particular your ISA allowance for this tax year.
Keep the money accessible. You did not want all of it locked away until a set age.

Your money comes from accumulated savings and a recent inheritance, both verified. You do not need access to the £100,000 for a specific planned purpose. You want it available if life changes, which is why accessibility matters to you and why it shapes the wrapper choice below.
Repaying debt first. You disclosed no liabilities on your fact find. There is no debt to repay ahead of investing, so investing the full £100,000 is appropriate.

Drivers for change. The money is currently sitting in cash. Over 22 years, cash interest has historically struggled to keep pace with inflation, so leaving it there risks a real fall in what it can buy. That is the driver for investing. No existing investment product is being replaced.
Your retirement position today
You asked whether £28,500 a year will be comfortable. Here is where that target sits.

The Retirement Living Standards, published by Pensions UK and researched by Loughborough University (updated 3 June 2026, retirementlivingstandards.org.uk), set out what different living standards cost in retirement. For a single person in London, a Moderate standard costs £34,000 a year and a Comfortable standard costs £47,200 a year.

Those are figures for net spending, not gross income. Your £28,500 target is a gross income figure. Using current allowances and tax rates, and assuming they do not change, £28,500 gross is about £25,300 a year net. That figure is derived, not measured.
Against the Moderate standard of £34,000, your target leaves a shortfall of about £8,700 a year. Your stated target is below a Moderate standard of living for a single person in London, not above it.
Three caveats matter:
The standards exclude rent and mortgage payments. They assume the home is owned outright. Your housing costs at 67 are not yet on file.
They exclude social care costs and financial support for dependants. You have one child.
I have used the London figures as the firm's default comparison. If you expect to retire elsewhere, the comparison changes.

This report does not tell you whether your provision will hit £28,500, because that needs a projection of your £111,226 pension, your State Pension entitlement and this new £100,000. I will complete that projection once the outstanding items are on file. Investing the £100,000 now is a step towards the target; it does not close a gap I have not yet measured.
Your investor profile
Attitude to risk

You completed the attitude to risk questionnaire and the result was Balanced. You confirmed that Balanced reflects how you feel about investment risk, so the risk level used for this recommendation is the same as the questionnaire result. No adjustment was made.

A Balanced investor accepts that the value of their investment will rise and fall, and accepts periods of loss, in exchange for the prospect of a better long-term return than cash. A Balanced portfolio holds a spread of shares, bonds and other assets, usually with a meaningful share in shares. You should expect falls in some years, including falls of more than a few percent. Over a 22-year term, you should expect several negative years along the way.
Investment timeframe

Your timeframe is 22 years, to your retirement at 67. This is a long-term investment. That length of term is what makes a Balanced level of risk appropriate: there is time for the portfolio to recover from falls before you need the money.
Capacity for loss
I assessed your capacity for loss separately from your attitude to risk, because they are different questions. Attitude to risk is how you feel. Capacity for loss is what you could actually absorb.

Your gross income is £47,500 a year and your regular outgoings are about £25,723 a year. You hold £10,867 in cash, about five months of outgoings, and that stays in cash. The £100,000 is surplus to that emergency fund and to your day-to-day needs. You confirmed you could tolerate short-term falls without changing your standard of living. A total loss would delay your retirement objective but would not derail it, because your pension of £111,226 and your State Pension entitlement sit outside this investment.
Your capacity for loss therefore supports a Balanced level of risk. There is no discrepancy between your attitude to risk and your capacity for loss, so no compromise was needed.
Vulnerability and capacity considerations

Nothing in our meetings or in your fact find indicated that you need extra support to understand or manage this advice. You are not in receipt of means-tested benefits, so this investment does not affect any benefit entitlement. You answered questions about risk and about your objectives clearly and consistently.
Tell me at any point if that changes, or if you would like this report in a different format, larger print, or explained again with someone you trust present. I am happy to do any of those.
Knowledge and experience, and responsible investing

You hold a workplace pension and have previously held a stocks and shares ISA. You understand that values fall as well as rise. You have no experience of complex or unregulated investments, and I have not recommended any. The recommendation uses a mainstream managed portfolio on a mainstream platform, which fits your level of experience.

We discussed responsible and sustainable investing. You told me you have no specific responsible investment requirement and asked for the standard approach. I have therefore recommended from the standard managed range rather than the responsible or sustainable ranges.
Your existing arrangements

Nothing is being replaced, switched or transferred. This recommendation invests new money. Your pension stays exactly where it is, in the same plan and the same funds. That has three consequences worth stating plainly:
There are no exit penalties, no loss of guarantees, no loss of loyalty bonuses and no market value reduction, because no existing plan is being given up.
There is no period out of the market while money transfers, because no transfer is taking place.
I have not cited poor past performance of any existing plan as a reason for this advice, so no performance comparison arises.

I will review the pension, its funds and its charges when I complete your retirement projection. That is why its provider details and charges appear in the outstanding items above.

My recommendation

I recommend you invest £98,000, after the initial advice fee, through the Quilter platform: £20,000 into a Stocks and Shares ISA and £78,000 into a General Investment Account. Both are invested in a WealthSelect Managed Portfolio matched to your Balanced profile.
Why the platform and wrappers are suitable for you

The ISA first. You have not used your ISA allowance this tax year. Inside an ISA there is no income tax and no capital gains tax on growth or income, and nothing to declare on your tax return. As a basic-rate taxpayer with a 22-year horizon, that is the most valuable allowance available to you for this money, so it is used first and in full.

The GIA for the balance. The ISA limit is £20,000 a year, so £78,000 cannot go into an ISA now. A GIA has no limit and no lock-in. Your capital gains tax annual exempt amount is unused, and each year we can move £20,000 from the GIA into your ISA. Over time that shelters the whole amount. You are responsible for your own tax return, and you should report any GIA gains or income to HMRC. If you use an accountant, share the annual tax certificate the platform issues.
Both on one platform. Holding the ISA and GIA together lets me move money between them each year, invest both in the same portfolio, and report on the whole £98,000 in one place.

The portfolio. The WealthSelect Managed Portfolio recommended is aligned to your Balanced profile. It is diversified across asset classes and rebalanced centrally, so it stays at your risk level rather than drifting. It comes from the Quilter Investment Matrix, which Quilter researches and monitors centrally. That central research is the research behind this recommendation, so no separate fund research report is required.
The term. The 22-year term matches your retirement at 67 and is what makes this level of risk appropriate. You are 45, so there is no life expectancy consideration that shortens the term.
Scope. The recommendation uses regulated, mainstream, readily realisable investments only. It includes no unregulated or non-mainstream investments, no share dealing and no investment trusts.

Affordability and good outcome. The £100,000 is surplus money. Your £10,867 emergency fund is untouched, your income of £47,500 covers your outgoings of £25,723, and you have no debt. Nothing here depends on you finding further money.
Taking an income

This section is not relevant to your case. You are not taking an income or withdrawals from this investment, and you are not accessing pension benefits. There is therefore no income sustainability assessment, no tax-free cash calculation and no money purchase annual allowance consideration in this report.
Investment fund recommendation

Other items to consider

Emergency fund. You hold £10,867 in cash, about five months of your £25,723 annual outgoings. That stays in cash and is not invested. I am satisfied that is an appropriate reserve for your circumstances. Review it if your outgoings rise.

Wills and estate planning. You have not told me whether you have a will. If you die without one, the law decides who inherits, which may not match your wishes, and you have one child. I recommend you put a will in place or review an existing one. Will writing is not regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority.

Lasting power of attorney. No lasting power of attorney is recorded on your file. Without one, if you lost the ability to make decisions, nobody could manage your ISA, GIA or pension on your behalf without applying to the Court of Protection. I recommend you consider both a property and financial affairs LPA and a health and welfare LPA. Lasting powers of attorney are not regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority.

Protection. You are self-employed with one child. Your protection needs are not covered by this report. I can review them at your next meeting.
Pension contributions. Investing this money in an ISA and GIA does not stop you making pension contributions from your income. I will look at that alongside your retirement projection.
How costs will impact your money

In pounds and pence, moving from cash to the recommended plan costs you £2,000 once, and about £1,921 in the first year, so about £3,921 in year one. Your existing pension charges are unchanged, because that plan is untouched.

The £980 is proportionate to that work and does not defeat the purpose of investing, because the portfolio is expected to grow ahead of total charges over the term. The firm's minimum ongoing fee for its entry service is £800 a year, so the percentage fee applies rather than a minimum.
